questions.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2}-1),4t-1⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v.$
questions.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2}-1)),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2}-1),4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+3),\,\sqrt{t}⟩,\,t>0.
$$

The speed at time $t=1$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+3)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t+3},\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=1,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1+3},\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{4},\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=1$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(1),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(1)| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{16}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To find the velocity when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ),4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨-4(0),4(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(\frac{\pi }{2})| & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}-4t+8),{t}^{4}-\frac{8}{3}{t}^{3}⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}-4t+8),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-\frac{8}{3}{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-4}{{t}^{2}-4t+8},4{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2(t-2)}{{t}^{2}-4t+8},4{t}^{2}(t-2)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{2(t-2)}{{t}^{2}-4t+8},4{t}^{2}(t-2)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2(t-2)}{{t}^{2}-4t+8}=0\, & ⇒\,t=2, \\ 4{t}^{2}(t-2)=0\, & ⇒\,t=0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=2$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨{t}^{3}-3t,\,2{t}^{2}+6t-3⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+6t-3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-3,4t+6⟩ \\  & =⟨3({t}^{2}-1),2(2t+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨3(t-1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3(t-1)(t+1),2(2t+3)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3(t-1)(t+1)=0\, & ⇒\,t=\pm 1, \\ 2(2t+3)=0\, & ⇒\,t=-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

There is no value of $t$ that satisfies both equations, so there are no stationary points.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-6{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)^{-1/2}\cdot 2t,3{t}^{2}-12t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}},3t(t-4)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}},3t(t-4)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}=0\, & ⇒\,t=0, \\ 3t(t-4)=0\, & ⇒\,t=0,4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$ at time $t=1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨12,6{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time
canonical_examples.problem:
The position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of a particle $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ at time $t > 0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 6t^2+2, 2t^3\rangle.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨12t,6{t}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=2$, we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨12(2),6(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨24,24⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=2$ we calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{v}(2),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{24}^{2}+{24}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2({24}^{2})} \\  & =24\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed when $t=2$ is $24\sqrt{2}\approx 33.94$ to two decimal places.

canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle t^2-2t, t^3-3t \rangle, \quad t\in[0,\infty).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,3{t}^{2}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2t-2,3{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-2 & =0\,⇒\,t=1, \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $t=-1$ is outside of the domain of $t,$ so we discard it. 

The solution $t=1$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only time when the object is stationary.
